Case study: Latent transition analysis of course engagement with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/case-engagement-transitions.Rmd
case-engagement-transitions.Rmd

Latent transition analysis (LTA) estimates the probability of moving from one latent profile to another between consecutive occasions (Collins & Lanza, 2010). With group classes, each class has its own starting distribution and its own transition matrix, so the classes separate students who differ in how their engagement changes from students who differ only in where it starts.

Data and model

engagement_momentum holds 1,310 course enrolments of 106 students, ordered within each student by sequence. The five indicators are simulated as continuous values on a log-activity scale and standardized within course. The data are synthetic and follow the design of the engagement studies of Saqr and López-Pernas (2021) and López-Pernas and Saqr (2024), which identified course-level engagement states with latent class analysis and followed students’ sequences of states across a program. In the simulation, each student follows one of three trajectories (engaged, fluctuating or mostly disengaged), each a first-order Markov chain over three engagement states (active, average and disengaged). Engaged students show momentum, in that an active course tends to be followed by another active course; mostly disengaged students show inertia, in that a disengaged course tends to be followed by another disengaged course. Three profiles and three student classes therefore match the structure from which the data were generated, and the evaluation vignette shows that the BIC selects the same numbers for the multilevel profile model.

For student ii at course position tt, CitC_{it} is the latent profile and GiG_i the student’s class. The model estimates

  • the initial probabilities δk∣m=P(Ci1=k∣Gi=m)\delta_{k\mid m}=P(C_{i1}=k\mid G_i=m),
  • the transition probabilities akl∣m=P(Ci,t+1=l∣Cit=k,Gi=m)a_{kl\mid m}=P(C_{i,t+1}=l\mid C_{it}=k,G_i=m), which sum to one across destinations ll,
  • and a Gaussian mean and variance for each profile and indicator.

The transitions are first order and homogeneous: the next profile depends only on the current profile and the student’s class, and the probabilities are the same at every position. Profile means and variances are shared across positions and classes, so a change of profile is a change of state. Indicators are independent within a profile under the default diagonal covariance. The fit can fail to reach the global maximum from a single start, and a transition that is rare within a class is estimated from little information; the expected count of each transition shows how much.

library(latents)
vars <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "active_days")

moves <- lta(engagement_momentum, vars, "student", n_profiles = 3,
             n_group_classes = 3, time = "sequence", n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
#> Warning: An initial, transition or group-class probability is at its numerical boundary; Wald
#> inference is withheld.
get_results(moves, "starts")
#>    start log_likelihood converged iterations error
#> 1      1          -7444      TRUE         43  <NA>
#> 2      2          -7444      TRUE         47  <NA>
#> 3      3          -7444      TRUE         30  <NA>
#> 4      4          -7444      TRUE         46  <NA>
#> 5      5          -7444      TRUE         26  <NA>
#> 6      6          -7444      TRUE         38  <NA>
#> 7      7          -7444      TRUE         30  <NA>
#> 8      8          -7444      TRUE         46  <NA>
#> 9      9          -7444      TRUE         30  <NA>
#> 10    10          -7444      TRUE         39  <NA>

All ten starts converge to the same log likelihood, so the solution is replicated within this seed’s starts. The warning reports that one estimated probability lies at its numerical boundary; the section on sparse and boundary estimates below identifies it.

The profiles

plot_profiles() draws the profile means across the indicators, and each line’s label gives the profile’s share of the enrolments.

plot_profiles(moves)

Profile 1 is the disengaged state, Profile 2 the average state and Profile 3 the active state, with means of days active of -0.960, 0.005 and 0.790 standard deviations from the course mean. The heatmap shows the same means as standard deviations from each indicator’s grand mean.

plot_profiles(moves, what = "heatmap")

The contrast between profiles is present on all five indicators, so the profiles differ in overall activity more than in its composition.

Where students start

In the "initial" table, probability is δk∣m\delta_{k\mid m}, the chance of starting in each profile. prevalence is the expected share of all of a class’s enrolments in that profile, across the whole history, and group_class_probability is the share of students in the class.

get_results(moves, "initial")
#>   group_class profile probability prevalence group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1      0.7461    0.82094                  0.2178
#> 2           1       2      0.1063    0.12384                  0.2178
#> 3           1       3      0.1476    0.05522                  0.2178
#> 4           2       1      0.3834    0.33770                  0.3408
#> 5           2       2      0.3665    0.37729                  0.3408
#> 6           2       3      0.2501    0.28501                  0.3408
#> 7           3       1      0.1451    0.10101                  0.4414
#> 8           3       2      0.2421    0.21144                  0.4414
#> 9           3       3      0.6128    0.68755                  0.4414

Student class 1, with 21.8% of students, starts in the disengaged profile with probability 0.746, and 0.821 of its enrolments are expected there over the whole history. Class 3, with 44.1% of students, starts in the active profile with probability 0.613, and 0.688 of its enrolments are expected there. Class 2, with 34.1% of students, starts across all three profiles, with probabilities 0.383, 0.367 and 0.250, and spends its enrolments in similar proportions. Class 1 is therefore the mostly disengaged class, class 2 the fluctuating class and class 3 the engaged class. In classes 1 and 3, the expected share of enrolments in the dominant profile exceeds the probability of starting there: over the program, students drift towards the state that their class favours.

How engagement changes

The "transitions" table gives akl∣ma_{kl\mid m} for every class and pair of profiles. stable marks staying in the same profile. expected_count is the posterior expected number of such transitions in the data, so it can be fractional, and it shows how much information supports each estimate. estimated = FALSE would mark a row the data cannot inform, because the profile is never occupied before a student’s last course; such a row holds uniform placeholder values. Every row is estimated in this fit.

get_results(moves, "transitions")

The transition plot draws each class’s matrix as a heatmap, with the origin profile in rows and the destination in columns.

plot_transitions(moves)

In class 1, a disengaged course is followed by another disengaged course with probability 0.904, estimated from 196 expected transitions, and an average course is followed by a disengaged one with probability 0.617 (from 34.7 expected transitions): disengagement has inertia, and the average state leads back into it. In class 3, an active course is followed by another active course with probability 0.808, estimated from 297 expected transitions, and an average course is followed by an active one with probability 0.473: engagement has momentum. Class 2 has no dominant transition; its largest probability, 0.566, takes an active course to an average one, and its other probabilities lie between 0.20 and 0.44. These are the patterns of the generating model, in which disengagement and activity persist with probability 0.85 in the corresponding trajectories, and the fluctuating trajectory moves between states with probabilities between 0.25 and 0.40.

Sparse and boundary estimates

Some estimates rest on little information. Students in class 1 rarely occupy the active profile, so its transitions out of the active profile rest on 16.0 expected transitions and those out of the average profile on 34.7. Its probability of moving from the average to the active profile is at its lower bound, which is why Wald inference is withheld for this fit. A probability near zero shows that the data carry little information about that movement, not that the movement is impossible: in the generating model, mostly disengaged students move from the average to the active state with probability 0.10. Estimates like these can also mean that the chosen number of classes divides the available transitions too finely.

Assigned sequences

The sequence plot shows each student’s modal profile at each course position, one row per student. Modal assignment discards classification uncertainty.

plot_sequences(moves)

get_results(moves, "sequence_summary")
#>   group_class groups observations mean_length median_length shortest longest complete gaps
#> 1           1     22          278       12.64          12.5       10      15        4    0
#> 2           2     39          473       12.13          12.0       10      15        3    0
#> 3           3     45          559       12.42          12.0       10      15        8    0

The summary gives the number of students and courses in each assigned class: 22 students with 278 courses in class 1, 39 with 473 in class 2 and 45 with 559 in class 3. Sequence lengths range from 10 to 15 courses, so the rows of the plot end at different positions. The long runs of the disengaged profile in class 1 and of the active profile in class 3 are the inertia and momentum of the transition table, seen in the individual histories.

Classification uncertainty 

get_results(moves, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         3    1310      252.04           0.8249
#> 2      groups         3     106       26.32           0.7740

Relative entropy is 0.825 for enrolments and 0.774 for students. The entropy plot shows, within each profile, how the per-case entropy contributions are distributed, and the posterior plot shows the posterior probability of each case’s assigned profile.

plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "entropy")

plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "posteriors")

Both levels retain uncertainty, so an analysis that replaces the posteriors by modal assignments treats some enrolments and students as more certain than the model estimates them to be.

Transition networks

get_tna() returns the marginal transition matrix as a model of the tna package (Tikka et al., 2025). It pools the posterior expected transition counts across classes and normalizes them, so it uses the estimated transitions, not transitions counted from modal assignments. get_group_tna() returns one network per class.

network <- get_tna(moves)
plot(network)

per_class <- get_group_tna(moves)
plot(per_class)

The class networks show the patterns of the transition table: a dominant self-loop on the disengaged profile in class 1, movement among all three profiles in class 2, and a dominant self-loop on the active profile in class 3.

Recovery of the generating structure

The same check against the generating states and trajectories as in the introductory vignette applies to the transition model.

get_results(moves, "assignments", data = engagement_momentum,
            truth = c("state", "trajectory"))
#>     assignment class      truth             value   n proportion
#> 1      profile     1      state            active   0    0.00000
#> 2      profile     2      state            active  37    0.06740
#> 3      profile     3      state            active 512    0.93260
#> 4      profile     1      state           average  30    0.09288
#> 5      profile     2      state           average 258    0.79876
#> 6      profile     3      state           average  35    0.10836
#> 7      profile     1      state        disengaged 418    0.95434
#> 8      profile     2      state        disengaged  20    0.04566
#> 9      profile     3      state        disengaged   0    0.00000
#> 10 group_class     1 trajectory           engaged   1    0.02326
#> 11 group_class     2 trajectory           engaged   4    0.09302
#> 12 group_class     3 trajectory           engaged  38    0.88372
#> 13 group_class     1 trajectory       fluctuating   1    0.02439
#> 14 group_class     2 trajectory       fluctuating  33    0.80488
#> 15 group_class     3 trajectory       fluctuating   7    0.17073
#> 16 group_class     1 trajectory mostly_disengaged  20    0.90909
#> 17 group_class     2 trajectory mostly_disengaged   2    0.09091
#> 18 group_class     3 trajectory mostly_disengaged   0    0.00000

The transition model recovers the states as well as the multilevel profile model does: 93.3%, 79.9% and 95.4% of the active, average and disengaged enrolments, against 92.9%, 79.9% and 94.7%. It recovers the engaged and mostly disengaged trajectories about as well (88.4% and 90.9%, against 86.0% and 90.9%), but the fluctuating trajectory less well (80.5%, against 95.1%).

Limitations

The model assumes constant transition probabilities across course positions, so change specific to one stage of the program is averaged over positions; the simulated data satisfy this assumption, but applied data need not. Transitions are between successive observed courses, which can differ in duration, content and assessment. Class differences describe patterns in engagement histories and do not identify their causes. Wald standard errors are withheld for this fit because class 1’s probability of moving from the average to the active profile sits at its lower bound, and the numbers of profiles and classes were not compared for the transition model here; enumerate_classes() with time compares transition models over a grid of profile and class counts. Transitions supported by few expected counts, such as those out of the active profile in class 1, should not be interpreted.

References

Collins, L. M., & Lanza, S. T. (2010). Latent class and latent transition analysis. Wiley.

López-Pernas, S., & Saqr, M. (2024). How the dynamics of engagement explain the momentum of achievement and the inertia of disengagement: A complex systems theory approach. Computers in Human Behavior, 153, 108126. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2023.108126

Saqr, M., & López-Pernas, S. (2021). The longitudinal trajectories of online engagement over a full program. Computers & Education, 175, 104325. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104325

Tikka, S., López-Pernas, S., & Saqr, M. (2025). tna: An R package for transition network analysis. Applied Psychological Measurement, 49(6), 326–328. https://doi.org/10.1177/01466216251348840
